title: Offshore Drilling Expanded to Atlantic, Pacific, and Arctic Waters
synopsis: On January 20, 2025, Trump signed Executive Order 14148 rescinding Biden's January 2025 ban on new offshore oil and gas development along most U.S. coastlines. On April 18, 2025, the Interior Department launched a new five-year offshore leasing program process. By October 2025, leaked documents obtained by the Houston Chronicle revealed plans to open the East and West Coasts to offshore drilling — including California coastal waters — for the first time since the 1980s, with Beaufort Sea sales slated for 2026 and East Coast sales opening in 2028. The Big Beautiful Bill (P.L. 119-21, signed July 4, 2025) mandated two oil and gas lease sales per year through 2040 in the Gulf of America region.

sources.title: Trump administration aims to auction offshore oil leases along U.S. coastlines that have been off-limits for decades - CBS News

title: Wildfire Policy Failure: Prescribed Burns Halved, Four Firefighters Dead
synopsis: In 2025, the U.S. Forest Service — having lost 16% of its workforce (5,860 staff) under DOGE cuts — reduced hazardous fuel treatment by 1.5 million acres compared to 2024, including cutting prescribed burns nearly in half from over 1.6 million acres to roughly 900,000 acres. Agriculture Secretary Rollins and Interior Secretary Burgum then ordered a sweeping 'full suppression' policy for 2026, abandoning decades of science-backed managed fire strategies. On June 27, 2026, four federal firefighters died when the Snyder Fire in Colorado overran their position. Trump created the U.S. Wildland Fire Service by secretarial order — pulling 3,900 Interior firefighters from six agencies — without congressional approval. By August 2026, millions of acres were burning across the West under unprecedented drought conditions.

title: Big Beautiful Bill Kills IRA Clean Energy Tax Credits
synopsis: On July 4, 2025, Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (P.L. 119-21), which repealed or sharply restricted nearly every clean energy tax credit enacted under the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act. The EV consumer tax credits (Sections 30D, 25E, 45W) were repealed for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025; the Residential Clean Energy Credit (solar, geothermal; Section 25D) was repealed for installations after December 31, 2025. The Joint Committee on Taxation projected the law would reduce federal clean energy expenditures by roughly $267 billion in consumer credits and over $48 billion in advanced manufacturing credits through 2033. Wind and solar projects were made ineligible for clean electricity investment and production tax credits unless entering service before January 1, 2028.

title: NOAA and Weather Service Gutted: 600 Experts Lost, Forecasts Degraded
synopsis: Beginning in early 2025, DOGE-driven cuts and buyouts eliminated approximately 600 National Weather Service employees — roughly 15% of the agency — including the bulk of its most experienced meteorologists and equipment technicians. By March 2025, the NWS had cut weather balloon launches at eight northern locations from twice daily to once daily due to staff shortages, degrading the upper-air data fed into national forecasting models. NOAA had nearly 300 fewer meteorologists and hydrologists at the end of May 2025 compared to January. A Kansas City tornado outbreak on April 13, 2026 was poorly predicted, with a tornado watch issued only 30 minutes before the first twister; meteorologists linked the failure to missing morning balloon data. Deadly July 2025 Texas floods raised further questions about whether adequate staffing could have prompted earlier warnings.

sources.title: NOAA layoffs: How Americans will feel the impact of Trump’s weather forecasting layoffs | CNN

title: US Becomes Global Climate Pariah: Absent from COP30, Sabotaging Deals
synopsis: In November 2025, the United States was absent from COP30 in Belém, Brazil — its first absence from a UN climate summit in three decades — after Trump withdrew from the Paris Agreement on January 20, 2025 and described climate change as the world's 'greatest con job' at the UN General Assembly in September 2025. The Washington Post reported the Trump administration was actively lobbying against global climate goals and using economic threats to undermine them. Sanctions threats against envoys near a landmark shipping pollution deal succeeded in blocking the agreement, moving Saudi Arabia to vote in lockstep with the U.S. Reuters reported China stepped into Washington's traditional role as climate leader. UN Secretary-General António Guterres personally addressed Trump from the final session: 'We are waiting for you.'

sources.title: With State Department negotiators fired, US will be unrepresented at COP30 | CNN

title: Harvard $2.2B Funding Freeze After Defying Trump Demands
synopsis: On April 14, 2025, the Trump administration froze $2.2 billion in multi-year grants and $60 million in contracts to Harvard University after President Alan Garber refused to submit to government demands including broad admissions overhauls, leadership reforms, and a requirement to report foreign students to federal authorities. The freeze marked the seventh time the administration had targeted an elite university, with six of the seven being Ivy League schools. The administration escalated further on April 17, threatening to revoke Harvard's ability to enroll international students — who comprise roughly 27% of its student body — and demanding records on visa holders' alleged illegal activities. The entire $9 billion in Harvard federal funding was placed under review, and Trump separately called for stripping the university's tax-exempt status.

sources.title: Trump froze Harvard's funding. Scientists say research could be set back years | AP News

title: Columbia Pays $221M Settlement, Surrenders DEI Programs to Trump
synopsis: On July 23, 2025, Columbia University agreed to pay $221 million — $200 million over three years in a general settlement plus $21 million to the EEOC — to resolve Trump administration federal investigations and restore access to $1.3 billion in frozen research funding. The administration had canceled $400 million in Columbia grants in March 2025, alleging the university failed to suppress pro-Palestinian protests. In exchange, Columbia agreed to ban race-based hiring and admissions, eliminate programs promoting DEI outcomes or quotas, create new faculty positions in Israeli and Jewish Studies, adopt the IHRA definition of antisemitism, and appoint new DEI compliance administrators. The deal was described by the White House as a 'road map' for extracting similar concessions from other universities facing funding threats.

sources.title: Columbia University reaches a deal with Trump to restore federal research funds | AP News

title: NIH Terminates ~2,500 Research Grants, Cuts $5 Billion in Funding
synopsis: Between January and June 2025, the Trump administration terminated approximately 2,500 National Institutes of Health research grants totaling nearly $5 billion, per Senate Appropriations Committee Vice Chair Sen. Patty Murray. A JAMA analysis covering just February 28 to April 8 documented 694 cancellations worth $1.81 billion, with the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases losing nearly $506 million alone. A federal judge in Boston ruled on June 16, 2025 that the NIH had violated federal law by arbitrarily canceling over $1 billion in grants due to perceived DEI connections, finding the government was 'bearing down on people of color' and LGBT people. The NIH simultaneously fired or pushed out nearly 5,000 employees, and the administration proposed slashing the agency's budget by $17 billion — a 38% reduction.

sources.title: Here Are the Nearly 2,500 Medical Research Grants Canceled or Delayed by Trump - The New York Times

title: NSF Cancels 1,000+ Research Grants Worth $739M, Halts All Funding
synopsis: In April and May 2025, the National Science Foundation terminated over 1,000 active research grants worth approximately $739 million, targeting grants related to DEI, misinformation and disinformation research, and environmental justice. More than 400 awards were canceled in a single batch on April 18–22, 2025, based on form letters stating the grants no longer 'effectuate program goals or agency priorities.' On April 30, NSF instructed staff to stop awarding all new funding and disbursing payments on existing grants with no stated timeline for resumption — a move that threatened to affect roughly 40,000 active NSF-funded researchers. NSF's director abruptly resigned on April 24, and a federal court in California issued a preliminary injunction on June 23 requiring reinstatement of grants to 45 institutions.

sources.title: National Science Foundation Terminates Hundreds of Active Research Awards

title: CDC Orders Withdrawal of Scientific Papers, Bans Unauthorized Publication
synopsis: On January 31, 2025, the CDC's chief science officer emailed all division heads ordering withdrawal of all papers submitted to external scientific journals for a political review to comply with Trump's executive order recognizing only two biological sexes. By February 13, the ban had expanded to all CDC research regardless of subject matter, with staff verbally instructed that no papers could be submitted to outside journals 'for the time being.' Political appointees at HHS simultaneously took control of the CDC's flagship Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, dictating content, withholding three completed studies on the H5N1 bird flu outbreak for weeks, and ordering unrelated wildfire-health studies rushed to publication at Trump's political direction. Journal editors publicly condemned the directives as illegal censorship, and multiple CDC scientists offered to remove their names from already peer-reviewed papers to allow publication.

sources.title: CDC orders pullback of new scientific papers involving its researchers, source says

title: Trump Signs Two DEI Executive Orders on Day One, Purges Federal Programs
synopsis: On January 20, 2025, Trump signed Executive Order 14173 ordering the termination of all federal DEI, DEIA, and 'environmental justice' offices, positions, equity action plans, and grants within 60 days, revoking foundational civil rights and affirmative action orders dating back to Lyndon Johnson. A follow-on order on January 21 revoked Executive Order 11246 — the 1965 order banning discrimination by federal contractors — and directed the Attorney General to identify up to nine civil compliance investigations targeting corporations, nonprofits, and universities with endowments over $1 billion for DEI practices. The Education Department dissolved DEI councils, placed all DEI-focused career staff on paid administrative leave, and archived hundreds of DEI resource materials the same day. The orders affected an estimated 45 federal DEI offices and an unknown number of federal contractor programs across the economy.

sources.title: Trump's orders to end DEI programs reflect his push for a profound cultural shift | AP News

title: Federal DEI Workforce Purge: All Diversity Positions Abolished Across Agencies
synopsis: Following Trump's January 20–21, 2025 executive orders, a January 24 OPM memo directed every federal agency to terminate all DEI-related offices and positions within 60 days and to begin issuing layoff notices immediately. The Pentagon abolished all 41 remaining civilian and military DEI positions — on top of 147 already restructured or eliminated under the FY2024 NDAA — for a total of 188 DEI-related jobs cut or restructured across the Department of Defense alone, per a Government Accountability Office report released April 17, 2025. The Defense Advisory Committee on Diversity and Inclusion, a congressionally chartered federal advisory committee, was simultaneously disbanded. Across the entire federal government, thousands of Chief Diversity Officers and DEI program staff were placed on administrative leave and subsequently terminated, and all DEI training contracts with external vendors were canceled.

sources.title: Trump directs all federal DEI staff be put on leave and eventually laid off | AP News

title: Education Dept Drops Book Ban Investigations, Ends Civil Rights Oversight
synopsis: On January 24, 2025, the Department of Education's Office for Civil Rights dismissed 11 pending civil rights complaints related to book bans in public schools, rescinded all prior guidance treating book removals as potential civil rights violations, and eliminated the Biden-era 'book ban coordinator' position. The department also dismissed 6 additional pending allegations and annulled a settlement agreement with Georgia's Forsyth County School District. On January 29, Trump signed a separate executive order cutting federal funding from schools teaching curricula labeled 'anti-American' or promoting 'gender ideology,' defining those terms broadly enough to encompass standard history and health education. PEN America had documented over 16,000 book ban attempts in public schools since 2021, with the vast majority targeting books by authors of color and LGBTQ+ writers.

sources.title: Education Dept. Ends Book Ban Investigations - The New York Times

title: Trump Defunds NPR and PBS; Congress Rescinds $1.1B for Public Broadcasting
synopsis: On May 1, 2025, Trump signed Executive Order 14290 instructing the Corporation for Public Broadcasting and all federal agencies to immediately cease all direct and indirect funding for NPR and PBS, alleging 'biased' reporting. The CPB, which distributes approximately $535 million annually to public broadcasters, was ordered to revise its community service grant criteria to prohibit any funds flowing to the two networks before June 30, 2025. On July 18, the House passed a rescission bill 216-213 — on strictly party lines — canceling $1.1 billion in already-appropriated CPB funding covering the next two fiscal years. On August 1, 2025, the Corporation for Public Broadcasting announced it would begin steps toward its own closure, marking the end of nearly 58 years of federally supported public broadcasting established under the Public Broadcasting Act of 1967.

sources.title: House approves Trump's $9B cut to public broadcasting and foreign aid | AP News

title: Title IX Reverted to 2020 Rules, Transgender Student Protections Stripped
synopsis: On January 20, 2025, Trump signed an executive order declaring only two biological sexes exist and directing all federal agencies to reinterpret sex-based statutes accordingly, explicitly rescinding 11 Biden-era Title IX guidance documents protecting LGBTQ+ students. On January 31, the Department of Education issued a Dear Colleague letter to all schools confirming immediate enforcement of the 2020 Title IX regulations — which exclude gender identity from sex discrimination protections — effective retroactively for all open investigations. On February 5, Trump signed an additional executive order directing the DOJ to enforce a ban on transgender girls and women in female school sports under Title IX, threatening federal funding cuts for noncompliance. Schools in 26 states that had already reverted under prior court orders were joined by every other U.S. institution, eliminating transgender bathroom access, pronoun policies, and harassment protections at federally funded schools nationwide.

title: USDA/RFK Dietary Guidelines Politicized; NIH Nutrition Research Gutted
synopsis: In March 2025, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins and RFK Jr. announced a 'line-by-line review' of the 2025 Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee's science report, with Kennedy pledging guidelines as short as four pages — compared to the prior 164-page document — potentially contradicting scientific consensus on saturated fats, seed oils, and red meat. The NIH's lead ultra-processed food researcher resigned in April 2025 after 21 years, citing fear of censorship. The Trump budget proposed cutting NIH nutrition research funding while also eliminating the CDC's National Center for Chronic Disease Prevention and Health Promotion ($1.4 billion annual budget). Scientists and CSPI condemned the MAHA Commission's strategy report for including fake citations and pseudoscientific claims, while the administration canceled over $1 billion in local food funding and terminated NIH grants covering nutrition and diet-related disease research.

title: Smithsonian DEI Purge: 32+ Artifacts Removed From African American Museum
synopsis: On March 27, 2025, Trump signed an executive order directing Vice President JD Vance to oversee elimination of 'improper, divisive, or anti-American' ideology across all Smithsonian Institution museums, specifically citing the National Museum of African American History and Culture (NMAAHC) for promoting 'divisive, race-centered ideology.' By late April and May 2025, NBC News documented at least 32 artifacts removed from NMAAHC galleries, including Nat Turner's Bible, items related to civil rights protests, and a diary tied to abolitionist history. The museum's director Kevin Young resigned in April after taking personal leave in March. Lenders of historically significant artifacts — including a Bible carried by Martin Luther King Jr. during protests, owned by civil rights leader Rev. Amos C. Brown — reported the Smithsonian unexpectedly ended their loan agreements early.

sources.title: Frustrations, fear of erasing history voiced after artifacts returned from African American history museum

title: Pentagon DEI Purge: 188 Positions Abolished, Advisory Committee Disbanded
synopsis: On January 27, 2025, Trump signed Executive Order 14185 directing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to abolish every DEI office within the Department of Defense, including all sub-offices, programs, and initiatives. According to a Government Accountability Office report released April 17, 2025, the DOD had cut or restructured 188 DEI-related civilian and military positions since early 2024. The congressionally chartered Defense Advisory Committee on Diversity and Inclusion was disbanded, and a Pentagon task force was created in February 2025 to oversee and certify the complete elimination of DEI activity across all military branches. By March 1, 2025, the task force certified no DEI goals remained in organizational composition, academic admissions, or career fields across any branch.

title: Penn $175M Research Halted; Stanford 82 Grants Cut; Universities Targeted
synopsis: In March 2025, the Trump administration issued stop-work orders on $175 million in federally contracted research across seven schools at the University of Pennsylvania, citing the university's 2022 allowance of a transgender athlete on the women's swim team — even though Penn stated it was already complying with the new Title IX rules. The halted contracts covered research on preventing hospital infections, drug screening against viruses, quantum computing, chemical warfare defenses, and student loan programs. Stanford University reported 82 federally supported grant terminations by September 2025, totaling $41.2 million. Dozens of other research universities — including Harvard, Columbia, Penn, and institutions across 26 states — faced NIH and NSF grant terminations as the administration used research funding as political leverage in a broader campaign against universities.

title: EPA, NASA, NOAA Scientific Advisory Committees Purged or Disbanded
synopsis: On January 28, 2025, EPA acting administrator James Payne dismissed all members of the agency's Science Advisory Board (SAB) and Clean Air Scientific Advisory Committee (CASAC) in a late-evening email, calling it a 'reset.' Both committees are legally required under federal law and had members with 2–3 years remaining on their terms. A broader executive order signed in February 2025 directed multiple agencies to identify advisory committees for termination; by March 20, NASA, NOAA, USGS, and other science agencies had moved to eliminate or consolidate more than a dozen science advisory panels. NSF announced closure of 12 advisory committees on April 15. CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices and FDA's Vaccines Advisory Committee had meetings canceled, severing decades-old independent scientific oversight.

sources.title: Acting EPA administrator moves to ‘reset’ to two scientific advisory committees : NPR

title: Big Beautiful Bill Medicaid Cuts: 10 Million Lose Coverage
synopsis: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (P.L. 119-21), signed by Trump on July 4, 2025, contains approximately $840 billion in Medicaid cuts over ten years. The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) estimated on July 21, 2025 that the law's health provisions would leave 10 million more Americans without insurance by 2034. The law's community engagement (work) requirements alone — which mandate that able-bodied, non-elderly adults prove employment, education, or community service to retain Medicaid — will reduce federal Medicaid outlays by $325.6 billion and cause 4.8 million people to lose coverage by 2034. An additional 1.3 million people with both Medicaid and Medicare would lose their Medicaid coverage. Democrats and health advocacy groups called the cuts the largest reduction to Medicaid in the program's 60-year history.

title: ACA Navigator Program Slashed 90%, Enrollment Rules Tightened
synopsis: On February 14, 2025 — the day after RFK Jr. was sworn in as HHS secretary — the Trump administration announced it would cut the ACA Navigator program from $98 million to $10 million annually, a reduction of $360 million over four years. Navigators are community-based organizations that help low-income and uninsured Americans enroll in ACA marketplace plans; in 2024 they served roughly 4.6 million people with counseling and enrollment assistance. The administration justified the cut by claiming navigators enrolled only 0.6% of marketplace selections at a cost of $1,061 per enrollment. In June 2025, CMS also finalized rules shortening the open enrollment window to end December 15 (one month earlier) and eliminating the monthly special enrollment period for those below 150% of the federal poverty line, which had been created to help the most vulnerable sign up year-round.

title: SNAP Food Stamp Cuts: 2.7 Million Lose Benefits Under OBBBA
synopsis: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act enacted on July 4, 2025 imposed the largest cuts to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) in the program's history, reducing federal SNAP spending by over $280 billion over ten years. CBO analyses released in August 2025 found that expanded work requirements will cause 2.4 million fewer Americans to receive benefits in an average month, including parents of dependent children newly subject to work mandates for the first time. An additional 300,000 people will lose benefits beginning in 2028 when states are required to share benefit costs, with some states expected to leave the program entirely. A cap on Thrifty Food Plan updates will reduce the average monthly benefit from a projected $227 to $213 by 2034. Groups most at risk include veterans, people experiencing homelessness, and young adults aging out of foster care.

title: RFK Jr. Runs HHS: Vaccines Undermined, Autism Commission, Raw Milk
synopsis: Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime anti-vaccine activist and founder of Children's Health Defense, was confirmed as HHS secretary on February 13, 2025, giving him oversight of the CDC, FDA, and NIH. Within his first month he canceled or postponed meetings of the FDA's independent vaccine advisory committee that selects flu shot strains, ordered CDC research into a debunked vaccines-autism link, endorsed unproven measles treatments (vitamin A, cod liver oil, steroids) over vaccination, and directed FDA to investigate GRAS food additive designations. Kennedy also recruited raw milk advocate Mark McAfee to apply for an FDA policy role and publicly promoted interstate raw milk sales despite CDC warnings that raw milk can carry H5N1 bird flu and pathogens linked to miscarriages and death. HHS announced in April 2025 it would launch a 'massive' autism research effort to determine causes by September 2025, driven by Kennedy's false theory that environmental toxins cause autism.

sources.title: RFK Jr.'s biggest challenges as HHS secretary: DOGE cuts and Trump's agenda

title: CDC Gutted: 20,000 HHS Jobs Cut, Surveillance Programs Eliminated
synopsis: In March 2025, the Trump administration announced the elimination of 20,000 HHS positions — roughly one-quarter of the department's total workforce — including thousands of CDC employees. An Associated Press investigation published May 4, 2025 found that more than a dozen data-gathering and disease-tracking programs had been effectively eliminated, including the WISQARS accidental-death and injury database, the AtlasPlus HIV/STD surveillance tool, and the 17-person team running the National Survey on Drug Use and Health. In July 2025, the CDC's FoodNet program — which had tracked foodborne illnesses for 30 years — was scaled back from monitoring eight pathogens to just two (salmonella and E. coli). The administration also proposed cutting CDC's core budget by more than half and pulled $11 billion from state and local health departments without warning in March 2025.

sources.title: Kennedy's 'MAHA' quest begins: 10,000 jobs expected to be cut at health agencies

title: NIH Research Gutted: 2,100 Grants Canceled, $12.1 Billion Terminated
synopsis: On April 1, 2025 — Jay Bhattacharya's first day as NIH director — the chiefs of four NIH institutes were placed on administrative leave, including the directors of NIAID, NICHD, NIMHD, and NINR, institutes collectively overseeing $9 billion in funding. By June 9, 2025, NIH staff published the Bethesda Declaration, an unprecedented public rebuke stating the agency had terminated 2,100 research grants totaling $9.5 billion and an additional $2.6 billion in contracts since Trump took office January 20. Canceled grants covered vaccine hesitancy research, LGBTQ+ health, gender identity studies, COVID-19 research, and environmental justice. Sixty-plus current NIH employees signed the letter warning the cuts 'harm the health of Americans and people across the globe' and 'waste public resources.' Researchers and universities sued NIH in April 2025 to stop further grant cancellations.

sources.title: Here Are the Nearly 2,500 Medical Research Grants Canceled or Delayed by Trump - The New York Times

title: SAMHSA Dismantled: $1.7B Block Grants Cut, Half of Staff Eliminated
synopsis: The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) was targeted for dissolution in 2025, with RFK Jr. announcing it would be absorbed into a new entity called the Administration for a Healthy America. Since January 2025, SAMHSA has lost more than half its approximately 900 employees. The agency terminated $1.7 billion in community mental health block grants to state health departments and cut roughly $350 million in addiction and overdose prevention funding. The Trump budget also proposed cutting an additional $1 billion from SAMHSA. These cuts came as overdose deaths in the U.S. had just fallen 27% in 2024 — an unprecedented decline attributed in part to programs SAMHSA supports, including the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, which served over 10 million people in its first year.

sources.title: Federal Agency Dedicated to Mental Illness and Addiction Faces Huge Cuts

title: Medication Abortion Under Siege: FDA Review, Comstock Threat
synopsis: In May 2025, HHS Secretary RFK Jr. directed the FDA to launch a safety review of mifepristone — the first medication in a two-drug regimen used in 63% of U.S. abortions — which experts warned could lead to tighter telehealth restrictions, mandatory in-person prescriptions, or removal from pharmacy shelves. As of July 2025, 12 states had total abortion bans and nine states explicitly banned telehealth-provided medication abortion. The Trump Justice Department was also weighing a broader interpretation of the 1873 Comstock Act that could ban mailing abortion pills nationwide regardless of state law. Texas in September 2025 passed a law allowing private citizens to sue physicians, manufacturers, and distributors from outside the state who mail abortion medication into Texas — a direct attack on blue-state shield laws. Louisiana grand-juried a New York doctor in January 2025 for providing telehealth abortions to a patient in Louisiana.

title: Title X Family Planning Freeze: 879 Clinics, 834,000 Patients at Risk
synopsis: On March 31, 2025, the Trump administration froze Title X family planning funding for 16 of 86 grantees, withholding more than $65 million that had been earmarked for contraception, STI testing, and cancer screenings at clinics serving low-income and uninsured patients. All nine Planned Parenthood federation affiliates with Title X grants were affected, as were seven other nonprofit grantees. KFF estimated 879 clinics in 23 states — 24% of all Title X clinics — were impacted, and up to 834,000 people could lose access to Title X-funded care. HHS cited unspecified civil rights violations and Trump's executive order barring benefits to undocumented immigrants but refused to detail the alleged infractions. By late April 2025, dozens of clinics had begun closing. Title X serves 2.8 million clients annually across nearly 4,000 clinics, with 83% of patients having family incomes at or below 250% of the federal poverty level.

title: PEPFAR and Global Health Cuts: HIV, Malaria Drugs Halted Worldwide
synopsis: Days after Trump's January 20, 2025 inauguration, USAID sent memos ordering contractors to immediately stop supplying HIV, malaria, and tuberculosis drugs — as well as maternal health and contraception supplies — to dozens of countries. On February 27, 2025, the administration terminated more than 90% of USAID programs after a 90-day 'America First' foreign aid review. UNAIDS documented that the sudden freeze caused immediate disruptions to antiretroviral therapy for millions of HIV patients across Africa, where PEPFAR had supported over 20 million people on treatment. A September 2025 Washington Post investigation found that shipments worth $76 million scheduled for delivery through June 2025 — including the majority of antimalarial medication for over 40 countries — were never delivered, leaving supplies stranded in ports and warehouses. Children died in some countries before drug supplies could be rerouted.

sources.title: Trump's 'stop-work' order for PEPFAR cuts off anti-HIV drugs for patients : Goats and Soda : NPR

title: Measles Epidemic: 700+ Cases, 3 Deaths, RFK Blames Everything but Vaccines
synopsis: In early 2025, a measles outbreak began in a tight-knit religious community in West Texas and spread across New Mexico, Oklahoma, and Kansas — ultimately becoming one of the worst U.S. outbreaks in 25 years with over 700 confirmed cases by April 2025. Three people died: two children in Texas and an unvaccinated adult in New Mexico, marking the first measles deaths in the U.S. since 2015. HHS Secretary RFK Jr. responded not with a unified call to vaccinate, but by promoting unproven treatments including vitamin A, steroids, and cod liver oil, writing in a Fox News op-ed that 'the decision to vaccinate is a personal one.' Scientists warned the U.S. was at a tipping point for the return of endemic measles — declared eradicated nationally in 2000. Kennedy also revived debunked claims in May 2025 that the measles vaccine contains 'fetal debris,' contradicting decades of evidence that the MMR vaccine is safe.

sources.title: RFK Jr.'s response to a deadly measles outbreak has doctors worried : NPR

title: Drug Pricing EOs: Biden Pilot Programs Killed, MFN Order Has No Teeth
synopsis: On January 20, 2025, Trump rescinded Executive Order 14087 — Biden's 2022 order directing HHS to develop new models to lower drug costs for Medicare and Medicaid patients, including a proposed $2 monthly cap on generic drugs. While the IRA's $35 insulin cap and $2,000 annual out-of-pocket cap remained intact as statutory law, the cancellation ended three CMS Innovation Center pilot programs before they could be implemented. On May 12, 2025, Trump signed Executive Order 14297 directing drugmakers to align U.S. prices with the lowest prices in comparable developed nations ('most favored nation' pricing); pharma stocks rose on the announcement as analysts and legal experts questioned how it could be enforced. Congressional Research Service analysis noted the order lacked defined legal authority and could conflict with existing IRA drug negotiation provisions. No major price reductions had materialized from the MFN order by August 2025.

title: Rural Hospital Closures: 300+ at Risk from $840B Medicaid Cuts
synopsis: A June 2025 analysis by the Cecil G. Sheps Center for Health Services Research found that over 300 financially struggling rural hospitals were at heightened risk of closure, service reductions, or ending inpatient care due to the OBBBA's Medicaid cuts. Nearly half of all rural hospitals were already operating in the red before the law's enactment, and the cuts were projected to drain $1.8 billion from rural hospital net revenues with a 15% Medicaid reduction. The law included a $50 billion, five-year Rural Health Transformation Program, but Health Affairs analysis found it was not required to flow to rural hospitals, was run by CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz with broad discretion, and expired after five years while Medicaid cuts were permanent. By early 2026, rural hospitals in Nebraska, North Carolina, New Hampshire, Minnesota, Virginia, and Oklahoma were closing services, with INTEGRIS Health citing a projected $130 million loss.

title: CHIP and Head Start Attacked: Children's Programs Slashed
synopsis: The OBBBA signed July 4, 2025 included provisions placing a 10-year moratorium on the Medicaid/CHIP Eligibility and Enrollment Rule, which had streamlined enrollment for over 37 million children covered by Medicaid and CHIP. Georgetown's Center for Children and Families found that 21 states covering lawfully residing immigrant children through separate CHIP programs face a penalty doubling their state share of costs unless they drop coverage. The Commonwealth Fund estimated 1 in 5 children could be at risk of losing Medicaid coverage under the bill's work requirements. Separately, Trump's April 2025 draft HHS budget proposed eliminating all funding for Head Start — a program providing early education to over 500,000 of the nation's most vulnerable children — arguing Congress should not fund it going forward.

sources.title: How Kids Are Harmed by Trump’s Budget Cuts — ProPublica

title: Opioid Treatment Programs Gutted as Overdose Deaths Were Falling
synopsis: In April 2025, a leaked Trump HHS draft budget proposed eliminating a $56 million annual SAMHSA grant program that distributed Narcan (naloxone) kits and trained emergency responders across the country — the primary tool credited with reversing hundreds of thousands of overdose deaths each year. This came immediately after CDC data showed overdose deaths had plummeted 27% in 2024, an unprecedented decline. SAMHSA also cut roughly $350 million in addiction and overdose prevention funding and terminated the 17-person team running the National Survey on Drug Use and Health, the only federal survey tracking drug use and addiction trends for over five decades. A Pennsylvania harm-reduction center that had distributed thousands of naloxone doses closed; Reuters reported that a narcotics-testing lab had furloughed chemists who tested the potency of illicit street drugs, eliminating critical intelligence for fighting the fentanyl crisis.

sources.title: U.S. overdose deaths fell again in 2025, but some worry about policy and drug supply changes | PBS News

title: Liberation Day: Trump's Global Tariff Shock Rattles World Markets
synopsis: On April 2, 2025, President Trump declared a national economic emergency and announced sweeping tariffs from the Rose Garden — a 34% rate on China, 20% on the European Union, 24% on Japan, and a 10% baseline on virtually all other nations, branding it 'Liberation Day.' Global markets reacted immediately: Japan's Nikkei dropped nearly 4%, Hong Kong's Hang Seng fell 1.5%, and U.S. Dow futures were down 2.5% pre-market. JPMorgan analysts warned the tariffs would impose a $660 billion annual tax increase on Americans, raise CPI by 2%, and likely push the U.S. and global economies into recession in 2025 — raising their recession probability estimate from 40% to 60%. EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called it 'a major blow to the world economy' with 'dire' consequences for millions of people.

title: Bond Market Panic Forces Trump to Blink: 90-Day Tariff Pause
synopsis: On April 9, 2025 — exactly one week after Liberation Day — Trump abruptly announced a 90-day pause on reciprocal tariffs for most nations, dropping rates back to 10% while simultaneously raising China's tariff to 125%. The reversal came after senior advisers Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick warned Trump that the bond market was in near-panic: 10-year Treasury yields surged to a seven-week high, the opposite of the normal flight-to-safety dynamic, threatening mortgage rates and business lending. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said Trump's market crash had 'vaporized a whopping $104,000 from the average retirement account.' title: US-China Tariff Spiral: 145% vs. 125% in Escalating Trade War
synopsis: Following the Liberation Day tariff announcement, the US-China trade war escalated in a rapid tit-for-tat spiral. By April 9, 2025, the White House confirmed total US tariffs on Chinese goods had reached 145% — combining 125% reciprocal tariffs with a preexisting 20% fentanyl-related levy. China retaliated on April 11, raising its duties on all US goods from 84% to 125%, effective April 12. China's Finance Ministry called the US policy 'a joke in the history of the world economy' and declared it would not respond to any further US tariff hikes. China filed a new WTO lawsuit against the US and rallied other trading partners against Washington. Analyst Victor Gao of the Center for China and Globalization warned that trade between the two largest economies 'will come to an abrupt halt in a matter of weeks' at those rates. title: Canada and Mexico Hit With 25% Tariffs Over Fentanyl Pretext
synopsis: On February 1, 2025, Trump imposed 25% tariffs on all goods from Canada and Mexico — the US's two largest trading partners under USMCA — citing fentanyl trafficking and illegal immigration as national emergencies under IEEPA. Canadian PM Justin Trudeau called the fentanyl rationale 'unjustified,' noting US customs data showed fentanyl seizures at the northern border had dropped to 'near-zero.' Mexico's President Claudia Sheinbaum announced 25% retaliatory tariffs on US goods, while Canada announced C$30 billion in retaliatory levies on US exports including OJ, wine, beer, coffee, appliances, and motorcycles. Canada subsequently added C$29.8 billion more in retaliatory tariffs targeting US steel, aluminum, and autos.

title: 25% Auto Tariffs Devastate Ford, GM, Stellantis: $108B in Costs
synopsis: Trump's 25% tariffs on imported vehicles took effect April 3, 2025, with 25% tariffs on auto parts set to follow by May 3. The Center for Automotive Research calculated the tariffs would increase costs for all US automakers by $107.7 billion in 2025 — $41.9 billion for Ford, GM, and Stellantis alone. Goldman Sachs estimated new vehicle prices would rise $2,000-$4,000; Cox Automotive projected a $6,000 increase for fully imported vehicles. Stellantis idled factories in Canada and Mexico making Chrysler and Jeep vehicles, laying off 900 US workers; Jaguar Land Rover suspended all US exports; Porsche halted European shipments. Analyst firm Telemetry projected upward of 2 million fewer vehicles sold annually in the US and Canada. Trump partially softened the tariffs April 29 by offering credits for domestically assembled vehicles, but core levies remained.

title: $6.6 Trillion Wiped From Markets in Historic Post-Tariff Crash
synopsis: The two trading days following Trump's Liberation Day tariff announcement — April 3 and 4, 2025 — produced the largest two-day S&P 500 market value destruction on record, surpassing even the COVID-19 crash of March 2020. The S&P 500 lost approximately $5 trillion in market cap by Reuters' count, with WSJ reporting a total of $6.6 trillion erased. The Dow Jones fell 1,679 points on April 3 alone, its biggest single-day drop since June 2020; the Nasdaq confirmed it entered a bear market, falling more than 20% from its December 2024 peak. Apple lost $315 billion in market cap in a single day — the second-largest single-stock decline on record. By the 100-day mark of Trump's second term, over $6.5 trillion had been wiped from public company valuations, making it the worst stock market start to any presidential term since Gerald Ford in 1974.

title: US GDP Contracts 0.3% in Q1 2025 as Tariff Chaos Hits Economy
synopsis: On April 30, 2025, the Commerce Department reported that US GDP contracted at an annualized rate of 0.3% in Q1 2025 — the first economic contraction in three years — reversing robust 2.4% growth in Q4 2024. Imports surged at a 41% annualized pace, the fastest since 1972 outside COVID disruptions, as businesses raced to stockpile before tariffs hit, mechanically subtracting 5 percentage points from headline GDP. Federal government spending fell 5.1%. Consumer spending slowed sharply to 1.8% growth from 4% the prior quarter. The Conference Board's Consumer Confidence Index had fallen for five consecutive months, with tariffs eclipsing inflation as the public's top economic concern; forward-looking components were already below levels historically preceding recessions. title: Tariffs Collapse US-China Shipping: LA Port Down 21%, Routes Axed
synopsis: The 145% US tariff on Chinese goods caused a sharp collapse in container shipping between China and the US in April-May 2025. title: Tariff-Driven Grocery Inflation Hits Fastest Pace Since 2022
synopsis: By August 2025, US grocery prices had risen at their fastest monthly pace since 2022, with the food-at-home CPI component jumping 0.6% in a single month, up 2.7% year-over-year, driven in part by Trump's tariffs on imports from China, steel, aluminum, and other nations. Coffee prices surged 20.9% year-over-year as of August 2025; uncooked beef steaks rose 16.6%; apples climbed 9.6%; bananas 6.6%. Yale University's Budget Lab estimated food prices would rise 3.4% in the short run and remain 2.5% higher long-run under Trump's tariff levels. title: Trump's $2.8T Revenue Claim vs. Economic Reality of Tariff Damage
synopsis: The Congressional Budget Office estimated in June 2025 that Trump's tariff increases implemented between January 6 and May 13, 2025 would reduce federal deficits by $2.8 trillion over 2025-2035 — but simultaneously reduce real US GDP by 0.6% by 2035 and lower the long-run growth rate by 0.06 percentage points annually. Trump repeatedly claimed the tariffs were generating record revenue and called them 'an American economic miracle.' In reality, by early 2026, the actual 2025 trade deficit in goods fell just 0.2% — not the '78% reduction' Trump publicly boasted — and the trade deficit in goods was actually up 2.1% compared to 2024. NBER economists calculated the average US tariff rate rose from 2.4% to 9.6%, the highest level of trade protectionism in 80 years, exceeding even the 1930s Smoot-Hawley tariffs as a share of GDP.

title: China Stops Buying US Soybeans: Farmers Face Five-Year-Low Prices
synopsis: China — which historically purchased at least a quarter of all US-grown soybeans — effectively stopped buying American soybeans in 2025 as a direct consequence of the trade war. In September 2025, China imported zero soybeans from the US, the first time in seven years that shipments fell to zero; for the first time in over 20 years, China did not buy from the autumn US harvest. Brazil captured an 85.2% share of China's soybean imports, with Chinese crushers booking 8 million metric tons of Brazilian beans for September alone. Chicago soybean futures fell to near five-year lows. In March 2025, China had already suspended soybean import licenses for three major US firms — CHS Inc., Louis Dreyfus Grains, and EGT — and imposed $21 billion in levies on US agricultural products including soybeans, wheat, meat, and cotton. US farmers were storing crops in hopes of a price recovery, delaying cash flow, while tractor makers and agricultural equipment businesses also suffered cascading losses.

title: Section 232 Steel and Aluminum Tariffs Doubled to 50% in June 2025
synopsis: On June 3, 2025, Trump signed a proclamation under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 doubling steel and aluminum tariffs from 25% to 50%, effective June 4 — on top of the February 2025 expansion that had already removed all country exemptions and raised aluminum tariffs to 25% globally. The 50% rate applied to all countries except the UK, which was held at 25% under the US-UK Economic Prosperity Deal. In August 2025, the Commerce Department added over 400 product codes to the tariff scope, including household appliances. By year-end 2025, US steel imports had fallen 21% compared to 2024 — from $31.6 billion to $24.8 billion — while aluminum imports fell 5% to $17.5 billion. The cumulative Section 232 tariff actions in 2025, combined with IEEPA-based universal tariffs, produced the most restrictive US trade policy since before World War II.

title: '90 Deals in 90 Days' Collapses: Only 2 Deals Reached by Deadline
synopsis: When Trump announced the 90-day tariff pause on April 9, 2025, White House trade adviser Peter Navarro boasted of '90 deals in 90 days,' and Trump himself claimed at his 100-day mark to have struck deals with '200 countries.' By the July 9 deadline, only two formal agreements had been reached — a partial framework with the United Kingdom and a preliminary deal with Vietnam. Trump then extended his own 'final' deadline to August 1, declaring 'no extensions will be granted,' only to extend it again. By July 9, 2025, CNN reported just three deals (UK, Vietnam, and China's partial 90-day tariff reduction), far short of the promised comprehensive restructuring of global trade. Foreign officials across 10 countries told Politico that negotiations were bogged down. The EU ultimately settled for a 15% tariff deal just days before August 1, with France immediately declaring it needed renegotiation.

title: Fed Refuses to Cut Rates as Tariff Stagflation Threatens Dual Mandate
synopsis: The Federal Reserve held its key interest rate unchanged at 4.25-4.5% at its May 7, 2025 meeting — the third consecutive hold — explicitly citing Trump's tariff-driven uncertainty as the reason it could not act despite presidential pressure to cut. Chair Jerome Powell warned that 'if the large increases in tariffs are sustained, they are likely to generate a rise in inflation, a slowdown in economic growth, and an increase in unemployment' — a stagflationary scenario that puts the Fed's dual mandate in direct tension. In congressional testimony on June 24-25, 2025, Powell stated he expected 'tariff inflation to show up more' in summer data and refused to signal a rate cut at any specific future meeting. Trump publicly demanded immediate rate cuts throughout this period, intensifying his conflict with the Fed's independence. Powell noted the 2025 tariffs were 'significantly larger than anticipated' and the situation was 'far from' the smaller 2018 tariffs that served as any historical guide.

India filed retaliatory duty proposals at the WTO in July 2025 over US auto tariffs affecting $2.89 billion of Indian exports, then faced an additional 25% US tariff on August 6 after trade talks deadlocked.
